clue.text: Two kings abducted from military quarters, written about for "The Talisman"

indicators.note: things abducted from a place are carried away from it, so those letters are taken out of the word
about here means turned round, so what remains is set down back to front

blocks.note: R (rex) and K are both abbreviations for king

explanation.surface: A tale of kings being snatched from barracks, written up as the plot of Scott's novel The Talisman.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking R and K out of BARRACKS leaves BARACS, which reads SCARAB backwards. The Talisman is a Walter Scott novel, a neat distraction from the lucky charm meant.
explanation.definitionFit: An Egyptian scarab beetle carving was worn as an amulet, a protective charm or talisman.

clue.text: See 18
For dressing down, tear clothing (formal article)

indicators.note: a garment clothing something wraps around it, so the bracketed words sit inside

explanation.surface: Someone getting a ticking-off for tearing a smart outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' tempts as clothing, but dressing down is one phrase for a scolding; the clothing is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dressing down is a severe scolding, which is exactly what a formal rebuke amounts to.

clue.text: Silky underwear?

blocks.note: setter's reading: belonging to a silk, a senior barrister (Queen's Counsel), whose instructions on a case come as written documents

explanation.walkthrough: A silk is a QC, a senior British barrister; the papers instructing a barrister share their name with a pair of short underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both close-fitting short pants and the case papers a solicitor sends to counsel.

clue.text: Tale-teller is conned, captivated by Henry's wife

indicators.note: something captivated by another is held captive within it

blocks.note: Catherine Parr, sixth wife of Henry VIII

explanation.surface: A storyteller swindled, having fallen under the spell of Henry VIII's queen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pardoner is one of the pilgrims who tells a story in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.

clue.text: Mental tranquillity, they say, is broken by one's severe 3

indicators.note: what people say is heard rather than read, so the phrase is taken by its sound
a phrase broken by something has that thing forced into the middle of it

blocks.note: calm of mind, then spelt as a fragment of it

explanation.surface: A calm state of mind, so the saying goes, shattered by a fierce telling-off.
explanation.walkthrough: PEACE becomes PIECE by sound, and ONE'S is pushed in before MIND.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving someone a piece of your mind is an idiom for a stern, angry rebuke.

clue.text: Scarlet sports car's interior to be made good

indicators.note: the inside of something is where these letters go, held within the colour

explanation.surface: A red sports car's upholstery being restored.
explanation.definitionFit: Losses recouped are recovered or compensated for, which is what making good a loss means.

clue.text: No dictionary included when writing about the theatre

blocks.note: a poem, a piece of writing
on a subject is about it

explanation.surface: Writing a review of a play without consulting a dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: An ode on something is writing about it. 'No dictionary included' is a nudge: O (no) and D (dictionary) open the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Odeon is a famous British chain of cinemas, a cinema being a picture theatre.

clue.text: In South Africa, do its inhabitants when climbing talk of the apples and pears?

definitions.text: do its inhabitants when climbing talk of the apples and pears?

blocks.note: first meaning: a port city on South Africa's Eastern Cape

blocks.clueFragment: do its inhabitants when climbing talk of the apples and pears?
blocks.note: second meaning: the part of London where Cockneys live, who use rhyming slang

explanation.surface: Wondering whether South Africans say apples and pears when going upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang, apples and pears means stairs; Cockneys come from the east of the British capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is shared by a South African coastal city and the Cockney heartland of the English capital.

clue.text: Gold captured by G-Grace, the swimmer

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor, so this sits within the other letters

blocks.note: the stammer before the word: its first letter repeated

explanation.surface: Gold medal won by a stammered Grace, the swimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: G-Grace shows a stutter, so the synonym is stuttered too: P-POISE, with OR inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A porpoise is a small toothed whale, a sea mammal that swims.

clue.text: See 13
Flinty queen stirred to embrace her husband? Not often!

indicators.note: a stirred mix is churned about, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: a queen's husband is the king, R for rex

explanation.surface: A cold-hearted queen moved to hug her husband: a rare event!
explanation.walkthrough: The king is folded into the anagram along with the queen's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done infrequently happens rarely or seldom, the plain sense of not often.

clue.text: Top Dutch gallery takes one pace back

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the word is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A leading Dutch gallery stepping back one pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like an adjective for the gallery but is a verb: to top someone is to kill them, here by beheading.
explanation.definitionFit: To top a person is slang for killing them, and cutting off the head literally removes the top.

clue.text: Female Spanish guerrilla, a revolutionary, points to Greek grub

explanation.surface: A woman fighter in Spain and a rebel directing people to Greek food.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is the crumbly white cheese of Greece, so it is Greek food, informally grub.

clue.text: Transient sailors, some Viking

blocks.note: some of the word: its last three letters

explanation.definitionFit: Fleeting means lasting only a short while, the same idea as passing or short-lived.

clue.text: For instance, seconds are 3ed

blocks.note: first meaning: seconds are counted away one by one, as by a clock

explanation.walkthrough: A clock's seconds tick away, so seconds are, for example, counted off on it; the same phrase is informal for told off.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ticked off is British slang for being rebuked, the same as being reprimanded.

clue.text: Ringing the draughtsman?

blocks.note: second meaning: read as two words, a man who draws up plans

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into PLAN GENT and it describes a draughtsman, the question mark flagging the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Plangent describes a loud, reverberating sound, often mournful, like a bell's peal.

clue.text: Mary does not take Ecstasy at Oxford

indicators.note: refusing to take something means leaving it out of the name

explanation.surface: Mary refuses drugs while at university.
explanation.definitionFit: Magdalen is one of the colleges of Oxford University, spelt without the final letter.

clue.text: At the double, double-jointed?

blocks.note: second meaning: two cuts of meat on the bone, a pair of joints

explanation.walkthrough: A chop is a small joint of meat, so two of them make something double-jointed in a butcher's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Chop-chop is a pidgin-derived interjection urging speed, matching the military command to hurry.

clue.text: Tale-teller exchanges chapter for small dish

indicators.note: exchanging one thing for another swaps them over in the name

blocks.note: Geoffrey Chaucer, author of The Canterbury Tales

explanation.surface: A storyteller trading a chapter for a little plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small dish' reads as one phrase, but small is the S swapped in and dish alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucer is a shallow piece of crockery that sits under a cup, a kind of plate.

clue.text: Software mogul ending off drinking mixed gins and swearing

indicators.note: with its ending off, the name loses its final letter
mixed drinks are blended together, so the letters are jumbled
someone drinking takes the liquid in, so these letters go inside

explanation.surface: A tech billionaire boozing on gin cocktails and cursing.
explanation.walkthrough: Billingsgate was London's fish market, whose porters were famous for foul language.
explanation.definitionFit: Billingsgate is a dated word for coarse abusive language, named after the market's porters.

clue.text: I head off home

blocks.note: surface reading: I set off for my house
setter's reading: the head of a college, whose official residence has a special name

explanation.walkthrough: At Oxbridge colleges the Master or President lives in the college's official house, so a head heading home goes there.
explanation.definitionFit: A lodge is a small house or a porter's or head's residence, so it is a kind of home.

clue.text: Swelling found as part of a nasty examination

indicators.note: found as part of means sitting inside the following words as a run of letters

explanation.surface: A lump discovered during an unpleasant medical check-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the edge of the eyelid.

clue.text: He'll take drivers round the course

definitions.text: He'll take drivers round the course

blocks.clueFragment: He'll take drivers round the course
blocks.note: surface reading: a chauffeur or racing guide ferrying motorists round a circuit
setter's reading: drivers are golf clubs, carried round a golf course

explanation.walkthrough: A driver is the long-hitting golf club, and the course is a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A caddie carries a golfer's bag of clubs round the links during a round.

clue.text: Only just beginning to look into each mixture

indicators.note: a mixture is things stirred together, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Just starting to examine every blend.
explanation.definitionFit: Inchoate describes something rudimentary, barely started or not yet fully formed.

clue.text: Lunatic intended, say, to get into the act

indicators.note: say asks for the word as spoken, so its sound is spelt another way
getting into something means going inside it

explanation.surface: Someone planning, so to speak, to join in the stage performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunatic and demented are synonyms describing someone behaving as if mad.

clue.text: Hard worker first struck the beam

indicators.note: the first letter is struck out, crossed off the front of the word

blocks.note: graft is British slang for hard work

explanation.surface: A diligent labourer who struck a girder.
explanation.definitionFit: A rafter is a sloping roof beam supporting the roof covering.
